introduction.Title: Introduction!
introduction.Body:
Welcome to my guide! My name is Lumpkinn, and I'm here to help you understand nodes in godot just a little bit better. This guide is going to cover the basics of 2D Nodes, 3D Nodes, Control Nodes, and show you a few more important ones. Keep in mind that the list and a ton of information about nodes change with the build of godot you're using, so always make sure to check the official documentation if there are any issues. 
 And with that, lets get started!
introduction.Tooltip: Throughout this guide, i'll be adding some extra info in the tooltips, so make sure to check them!

BasicsInfo1.Title: What are Nodes?
BasicsInfo1.Body: Nodes in Godot are kind of like building blocks. They all have their own purposes, and each of them serve a specific function in a project. The main parts that each node have are a name, and a type. You typically also have parent-child relationships between nodes as well, for both functionality, and organizational purposes. All nodes are born from the base type 'Node'. You can also attach a script to the nodes as well, allowing you to give it custom behaviors.
BasicsInfo1.Tooltip: If you've used nodes in another game engine, they're kind of the same here in godot! just make sure to check the documentation for any fringe cases!

BasicsInfo2.Title: Why are they important?
BasicsInfo2.Body: Nodes basically are the most central part of the engine. Think of them like templates for doing certain actions. If you didn't have that template, you'd have no idea on how to accomplish certain things.

BasicsInfo3.Title: How do I I use them?
BasicsInfo3.Body: To add nodes, you can either hit the plus symbol in the top left corner of the engine, or you can use the shortcut ctrl-a to automatically open up the node selection menu. From there, search for the node that you want, and add it to the project. From there, you can either click on the nodes to change certain things about them, or go to the inspector window on the right of the screen to ecit its properties.

BasicInfo4.Title: The Scene tree
BasicInfo4.Body: All of the currently active nodes that you're using are located in something called the scene tree. The scene tree holds all of your nodes, and lets you organize them in parent-child relationships. It bascially acts as a container for you to hold all of your nodes.
BasicInfo4.Tooltip: There is quite a bit more to know about the Scene tree. We'll be referencing it later on in the guide, and if you still have issues with it after, make sure to check the documentation!

TypeInfo1.Title: 2D Nodes?
TypeInfo1.Body:
Godot splits its nodes into three main groups, 2D Nodes, 3D Nodes, and Control Nodes. There are other nodes that don't fit into this system however, and for the purposes of this tutorial, I will be reffering to them as miscallaneous nodes. 
 This part of the guide will be focusing on 2D nodes specifically. 
 All 2D nodes fit under the most basic form of Node, which is incidentally just called '2D Node'. After that, it branches out into a multitude of different types of nodes. All of these nodes are specifically made for making a 2D game, with some examples being 'CollisionBody2D', which creates collision on a 2D plane. There are a ton more nodes under this category, and some are for stuff like lighting and sound
TypeInfo1.Tooltip: Make sure to check the documentation to see what specific nodes do!

TypeInfo2.Title: 3D Nodes
TypeInfo2.Body: The next group of nodes that'll be covered will be 3D Nodes. 3D nodes are practically the same as 2D Nodes, but adapted for a 3D project. For example, a CollisionBody 3D Node accomplishes the same thing that a CollisionBody 2D node does, it just adds an extra axis. There are some
TypeInfo2.Tooltip: Feel free to check the documentation for the specifics on these nodes!

TypeInfo3.Title: Control Nodes?
TypeInfo3.Body: Control nodes are a little special. They're mainly used for things like a games UI, settings, and menus. For example, this guide was made with mostly control nodes! They also have a special formatting system, which focuses on their position inside of another control node called a container. These containers control how the elements are stored as well!
TypeInfo3.Tooltip: There are tons of free resources for using control nodes, and i suggest that you take a look at them, mostly because we'd be here all day if i tried to explain them.

TypeInfo4.Title: Miscallaneous Nodes?
TypeInfo4.Body:
There are a ton of nodes in Godot that don't really fit into the classification system that i've made. So, this section of the guide serves to shed a bit of light on them. 
 Typically, these nodes are for universal functions that you'd need across all three aforementioned groups. One such example would be a timer. For example, you could use a timer in a 2d platformer to create urgency. You could also use it in a 3d game as a sort of confirmation, and you could also use it in a settings menu to revert settings if the user doesn't confirm them. All of these nodes are able to fit throughout the multiple different systems you'd find throughout Godot, and thus, they aren't in any specific group.
TypeInfo4.Tooltip: Once again, go check the documentation if you need some more info.

BasicUsageInfo1.Title: When to use 2D Nodes?
BasicUsageInfo1.Body: 2D nodes in Godot are pretty obviously going to be used whenever you make a 2D game. But a ton of them have specific use cases for 2D development. For example, take the two nodes CharacterBody 2D, and RigidBody 2D. They both can be used for creating a player character, but the RigidBody2D is better suited for physics objects, as opposed to the CharacterBody2D.
BasicUsageInfo1.Tooltip: There are a ton more examples of this, so make sure to compare the two, and see which one fits your use case better.

BasicUsageInfo2.Title: When to use 3D Nodes?
BasicUsageInfo2.Body: It's essentially the same issue that you'll see with 2D nodes. If you'd like a similar example, we can use the CSG nodes. These nodes are pretty good for prototyping, but not the best when you're intrested in pushing a finished project.

BasicUsageInfo3.Title: When to use Control Nodes?
BasicUsageInfo3.Body: Control Nodes are pretty much made for GUI elements, and settings. Whenever you want something displayed on the screen, you should probably go look at some control nodes.

CodeAndNodesInfo1.Title: Making Nodes with code.
CodeAndNodesInfo1.Body:
Sometimes while you work in Godot, you'll need to make nodes programically for a plethora of reasons. Like one example could be using it to create an effect. 
 To make nodes programmically, its as simple as creating a new instance by calling the name of the node (for example, Sprite2D), and call the method .new(). Make sure to assign this to a variable for future use. After that, make sure to add it to the node tree by calling add_child(), and include the variable name of the node within the parenthesis.
CodeAndNodesInfo1.Tooltip: .new() and add_child() haven't really been tweaked in a bit, so they shouldn't cause any issues if you use them properly. If there are any issues, go look at the documentation.

CodeAndNodesInfo2.Title: Referencing nodes from the scene tree
CodeAndNodesInfo2.Body: If you want your scripts to effect your nodes, you'll have to reference them in the script somehow. You've got two main ways to go about this. One way, which I think is the easiest is using the '$' notation. To do this, type out the path to the node, and add a $ right before the path. You can also assign this to a variable to make it easier for yourself. The other method is using get_node(). Pass the path to the method, and then you've got the node.

CodeAndNodesInfo3.Title: Removing nodes from memory
CodeAndNodesInfo3.Body: While you work on your project, you pretty obviously want it to not take too much of a toll on the hardware. And to do that, you'll want to use the memory efficently. One easy way to minimize memory use is removing nodes from the scene tree, which you can do in two main ways. One way, which is the golden standard for removing nodes is the method queue_free(), which puts all the nodes that you want removed that frame in order, and removes them after they've done everything they needed to do. The other method is just free(), which immediately removes the node, and sets all of its references to null, which may cause some issues.

NodesSignalInfo1.Title: What are signals?
NodesSignalInfo1.Body: While you work on your project, you might want two different nodes to share data. Like having something happen when you press a button. To do this, you'll need to use signals. A really stupid way to visualize it that I like to use is imagining a node screaming into the void. If you tell another node to listen for the first node screaming, he'll hear it, and know that he has to do something. Thats basically how nodes work.

NodesSignalInfo2.Title: Using Signals
NodesSignalInfo2.Body: If you want to use a signal, you'll need to first select the node that you want to use in the scene tree, and then after you select it, go over to the other side of the screen where the inspector is. Press on the signal tab at the top of the inspector panel, and you'll be in the signals menu. Pick the signal you want by clicking on it, and choose the script you want to use. Doing this will open the script, and will create a new method with a green symbol next to it. Now, whenever that signal is called, that method will run.

NodesSignalInfo3.Title: Signals and bind()
NodesSignalInfo3.Body: Lets say that you have a ton of buttons in your scene, and you want each button to do something unique. You could just make one signal for each button, and then repeat it for each method, but that isn't too good of a use of your time. To solve this issue, you'll have to use the .bind() method. Bind() basically lets you get a connect a value to each instance of a node, which you can then use to make specific things happen based off of the node itself.

CustomNodes1.Title: Can I make my own nodes?
CustomNodes1.Body: In Godot, you'll occasionally need to make your own nodes for a multitude of reasons. Maybe one node doesn't go as indepth as you might need it to. Maybe you need a specialized node for something. Well, as long as you're ok with writing a bit of code, you can make your own nodes!
CustomNodes1.Tooltip: This stuff is pretty advanced. Make sure to ask for help if you get stumped.

CustomNodes2.Title: Making custom nodes.
CustomNodes2.Body: To start making a custom node, you'll need to let godot know that you're trying to make a custom node, and to do so, you need to add the access modifier '@tool'. After that, you need to make the code extend EditorPlugin, and then define a class. After that, the implementation is up to you.
CustomNodes2.Tooltip: Make sure that your code is clean and readable so it'll be easy to write documentation for the code.

CustomNodes3.Title: Using your custom node
CustomNodes3.Body: To use your custom node, you can go to the node menu and grab it from there. If you want to change certain values about it in code, add '@export' infront of the variable definition.
